items.title: Adam Smith warned against corporate collusion
items.claim: Adam Smith is often invoked as a free-market champion. What did he actually say about businessmen meeting together?

options.text: That free assembly among capitalists is the engine of innovation
That 'People of the same trade seldom meet together... but the conversation ends in a conspiracy against the public, or in some contrivance to raise prices.'
That competition is a myth used by economists
Nothing — he never discussed business behaviour

items.reveal:
The quote is from The Wealth of Nations (1776), Book I, Chapter X. Smith was deeply suspicious of merchant power and joint-stock companies. He criticised the East India Company at length and warned that 'the proposal of any new law or regulation of commerce which comes from this order ought always to be listened to with great precaution.'

The 'invisible hand' appears only three times in his works, with a meaning closer to 'unintended consequences of self-interested behaviour, when channelled by competition' than 'markets always good'.
items.why: Smith is invoked rhetorically by people who haven't read him. The actual Wealth of Nations is alert to monopoly, collusion and the political power of capital — closer to a regulatory liberal than a libertarian.

items.title: The Phillips curve broke down spectacularly in the 1970s
items.claim: Bill Phillips's 1958 paper documented an inverse relationship between UK unemployment and wage inflation. What happened in the 1970s?

options.text: The relationship held perfectly, vindicating Keynesian demand management
The US and UK experienced 'stagflation' — high inflation AND high unemployment simultaneously, which the simple Phillips curve said was impossible
The relationship inverted entirely; lower unemployment led to deflation
Statistical data became unreliable, so no test was possible

items.reveal:
The 1970s combined oil shocks (1973, 1979), wage-price spirals and weak productivity growth. US inflation reached 13.5% in 1980; unemployment was 7.5%. Both up, together.

Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps had argued in the late 1960s that the long-run Phillips curve was vertical at the 'natural rate' of unemployment — once expectations adjusted, only the natural rate was stable. The 1970s vindicated them and supplied the intellectual ammunition for monetarism, Volcker and Thatcher.

Modern expectations-augmented Phillips curves are still used but are far less crisp than the original.
items.why: The Phillips curve example is the cleanest case of a model that worked, then didn't. It's also why mid-20th-century Keynesianism gave way to monetarism, with consequences that still shape macro policy.

items.title: The Soviet economy grew faster than the US for decades
items.claim: From the 1928 first Five-Year Plan to the late 1960s, how did Soviet growth compare to US growth?

options.text: The Soviet economy was always smaller and grew more slowly than the US
Soviet GDP growth averaged roughly 5-6% annually through the 1950s, faster than the US in the same period — before stagnating sharply in the 1970s-80s
Soviet GDP collapsed in 1932 and never recovered
The Soviet economy never produced reliable statistics

items.reveal:
CIA estimates put Soviet GDP growth at 5.7% (1950s) and 5.2% (1960s), against US rates of 3-4%. The growth was 'extensive' — pulling labour out of agriculture, building heavy industry, exploiting massive natural resources — rather than 'intensive' productivity gains.

By the 1970s the extensive sources were exhausted. Innovation faltered, oil propped up the system in the 1970s, then the 1980s collapse came when oil prices fell and reform under Gorbachev destabilised what remained.

Robert Allen, Stephen Kotkin and others have documented this trajectory in detail.
items.why: 'Communism never works' as a one-liner ignores 40 years of measurable, fast growth. The interesting question is why the model worked for extensive industrialisation but failed at the next stage.

items.title: Behavioural economics dismantled the rational agent
items.claim: Kahneman and Tversky's 1979 paper on Prospect Theory introduced a different model of choice. What's the key finding?

options.text: People are perfectly rational expected-utility maximisers
People weigh losses roughly twice as heavily as equivalent gains, and evaluate outcomes relative to a reference point rather than in absolute terms
People only care about wealth, never relative position
Rational choice perfectly predicts behaviour once information costs are included

items.reveal:
Prospect Theory (Kahneman & Tversky, Econometrica, 1979) replaced expected utility's smooth concave function with a kinked value function — steeper for losses than for gains — and replaced objective probabilities with subjective decision weights that overweight small probabilities.

Kahneman won the 2002 Nobel; Tversky had died in 1996 (the prize is not awarded posthumously). Richard Thaler extended the work into 'nudge' policy; Esther Duflo and others into development economics.

The homo economicus of textbook microeconomics still appears in models — but is now understood as an idealisation, not a description.
items.why: Microeconomics taught as if people are rational misrepresents both the discipline and the actual evidence. The behavioural turn is one of the most important shifts in economics in 50 years.

items.title: Almost no professional forecaster saw 2008 coming
items.claim: After the 2008 financial crisis, the Queen famously asked LSE economists why no one saw it coming. What's the accurate picture?

options.text: Most leading economists predicted the crisis from the early 2000s
A small number of analysts (Raghuram Rajan, Nouriel Roubini, Steve Keen, Brooksley Born, Michael Burry) warned about systemic risk; the consensus, including the IMF and most central banks, did not
The IMF published a precise prediction in 2006
The crisis was a complete surprise that no one anywhere foresaw

items.reveal:
Rajan's 2005 Jackson Hole paper ('Has Financial Development Made the World Riskier?') was dismissed by Larry Summers. Roubini was nicknamed 'Dr Doom' for warnings from 2006. Steve Keen had modelled private debt dynamics. Michael Burry famously bet against subprime (Big Short). The Bank for International Settlements raised flags.

Macroeconomic models in use (DSGE) had no banking sector and no default. The Queen's 2008 question to LSE got a follow-up letter (2009) from leading British economists admitting a 'failure of the collective imagination of many bright people... to understand the risks to the system as a whole.'
items.why: Economics' forecasting record isn't great — but the deeper issue was that mainstream models couldn't even represent the relevant risks. Heterodoxy isn't always wrong.

items.title: Tulip mania was less extreme than the legend
items.claim: Charles Mackay's 1841 'Extraordinary Popular Delusions' painted 17th-century Dutch tulip mania as a society-wide frenzy that crashed the economy. What does modern research find?

options.text: The crash bankrupted the Dutch Republic for a generation

Trading was confined largely to a small group of professional florists meeting in taverns; while bulb prices rose sharply and crashed in February 1637, the macro impact was modest and Mackay's tales of devastated cobblers are mostly unverified
Tulip mania never happened; it is a complete fabrication
It triggered the Eighty Years' War

items.reveal_title: A bubble, but a smaller one
items.reveal:
Anne Goldgar's 'Tulipmania' (2007) used archival records to show that bulb trading was largely among well-off merchants, that few contracts were ever actually enforced after the February 1637 crash, and that contemporary Calvinist moral pamphlets exaggerated the social ruin for didactic purposes.

Peter Garber argued similarly from an economist's perspective: peak prices for rare bulbs may have reflected genuine scarcity and fashion premiums, not pure delusion.

Mackay's account was readable, lurid and influential — but not historical.
items.why: Pop economic history is full of morality tales. The actual record is usually messier and less satisfying — but it's what students of bubbles need to grapple with.

items.title: The Great Moderation ended in 2008
items.claim: From roughly 1985 to 2007, US and UK output volatility fell substantially compared to earlier decades. What did Ben Bernanke call this period in 2004?

options.text: The Lost Decade
The Great Moderation — and Bernanke credited a combination of better monetary policy, structural changes (services, JIT) and good luck. The period ended emphatically with the 2008 crisis
The Roaring Eighties
The Macro Miracle

items.reveal_title: Stability that turned out not to be
items.reveal:
Bernanke's 2004 speech 'The Great Moderation' attributed reduced volatility to improvements in policy. The 2008 crisis suggested 'good luck' had played a larger role than recognised.

Hyman Minsky's earlier 'financial instability hypothesis' argued that stable periods breed speculative behaviour that ultimately destabilises the system — the 'Minsky moment' became a widely used term after 2008.
items.why: Periods of low volatility can mask growing fragility. Confidence in macroeconomic stability before 2008 was substantial; the consensus was wrong.

items.title: Potential GDP is not directly observable
items.claim: The output gap is actual GDP minus potential GDP, expressed as a percentage of potential. Why is this concept difficult to use in practice?

options.text: Output is impossible to measure

Potential GDP is unobservable — it must be estimated, and estimates are revised heavily after the fact. Pre-2008 estimates of potential GDP have been revised down substantially, suggesting the economy was less overheated than thought
It is observable directly from satellite
It is fixed at 3% annually

items.reveal_title: A concept whose measurement is treacherous
items.reveal:
OECD, IMF and central bank estimates of potential GDP use filters (Hodrick-Prescott, Kalman) and production function approaches. They produce different numbers and revise heavily as data arrives.

Orphanides's 2003 paper showed that real-time output gap estimates available to the Fed in the 1970s were systematically wrong, contributing to policy errors.

The BIS has criticised reliance on output gaps for monetary policy.
items.why: Policy variables that depend on unobservable concepts inherit estimation uncertainty. Output gap-based 'rules' look cleaner in textbooks than in practice.

items.title: Quantitative easing is not 'printing money'
items.claim: Central banks engaged in QE after 2008 and again in 2020-21. Which describes the operation most accurately?

options.text: Central banks printed physical banknotes and gave them to households
Central banks created reserves electronically and used them to buy government bonds (and other assets) from financial institutions; reserves are central bank liabilities, not currency in circulation
Central banks deleted money
QE doubled the M2 money supply directly

items.reveal:
By 2022, the Bank of England's gilt holdings under QE reached £895bn; the Fed's balance sheet peaked near $9 trillion. The reserves created are held by banks at the central bank; they don't enter the real economy as cash.

The mechanism is meant to lower long-term interest rates, support asset prices and ease financial conditions. Whether QE caused 2021-22 inflation is debated; the consensus is the energy shock and pandemic supply disruptions were the dominant drivers, with QE perhaps contributing at the margin.
items.why: 'Printing money' is a misleading shorthand for QE that conflates electronic reserve creation with currency issuance. The mechanisms have different implications.

items.title: Japan's debt-to-GDP is over 250% — and it hasn't defaulted
items.claim: Japan's general government gross debt was around 263% of GDP in 2023 (IMF). What's the orthodox explanation for why this hasn't triggered a sovereign debt crisis?

options.text: Japan does not actually have debt

Debt is mostly held domestically (BOJ, pension funds, banks) in yen, with the BOJ controlling the curve; net debt is lower; current account surplus; large household savings. Foreign-currency emerging market debt is structurally different
Japan secretly receives IMF support
Japanese debt is not real

items.reveal_title: Composition matters as much as level
items.reveal:
Reinhart and Rogoff's controversial 2010 'Growth in a Time of Debt' suggested debt above 90% of GDP harmed growth. Subsequent re-analysis (Herndon, Ash, Pollin 2013) found an Excel error and weaker results. The relationship between debt levels and outcomes depends heavily on currency denomination, holders, monetary regime and growth rates.

Greece (2010-12) and Sri Lanka (2022) had foreign-currency exposure that Japan lacks. The UK has a Liability Driven Investment (LDI) crisis in autumn 2022 despite much lower debt levels — composition and confidence matter.
items.why: Headline debt-to-GDP misleads about sustainability. Currency, holders, maturity profile, monetary regime and growth trajectory matter as much as the ratio itself.

items.title: Helicopter money was Friedman's thought experiment
items.claim: Milton Friedman's 1969 paper 'The Optimum Quantity of Money' used a vivid metaphor for direct money creation. What was it?

options.text: An infinite faucet
A helicopter dropping money from the sky for citizens to pick up — direct money creation transferred to households, bypassing the banking system
A bank vault opening
Friedman never proposed any such thing

items.reveal:
Friedman used 'helicopter money' as a thought experiment, not a policy recommendation. After 2008, with interest rates at the zero lower bound, the concept returned in policy debates — Adair Turner's 'Between Debt and the Devil' (2015), Bernanke's discussion of overt monetary financing.

Pandemic stimulus cheques (US 2020-21, Hong Kong, Singapore) were quasi-helicopter — fiscal transfers funded by debt the central bank was buying. The line between 'fiscal stimulus financed by QE' and 'monetary financing' became thin.
items.why: Macroeconomic terminology shapes what counts as orthodox or unorthodox. Many post-2008 interventions blurred categories that pre-2008 textbooks kept distinct.

items.title: The Bank of England became independent in 1997
items.claim: Gordon Brown announced operational independence for the Bank of England in May 1997, days after Labour's election victory. What's the standard rationale?

options.text: To allow politicians to set interest rates directly

To insulate monetary policy from short-term political pressure, given evidence that independent central banks (Bundesbank, Fed) had lower average inflation. The Treasury sets the target; the Bank sets rates
Because the Bank requested independence
To eliminate inflation forever

items.reveal:
Alesina and Summers (1993) had documented the inverse correlation between central bank independence and inflation across OECD countries. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand's 1989 Act pioneered explicit inflation targeting.

UK target: 2% CPI from 2003 (RPIX 2.5% before). The MPC has 9 members, votes monthly. Brown's surprise announcement preceded the post-1997 inflation stability period.

Independence has been challenged in some quarters since 2010s rate decisions; the Bank's bond buying in autumn 2022 (LDI crisis) raised questions about coordination with Treasury.
items.why: Institutional design — who decides what, accountable to whom — is as much a part of macroeconomic policy as the decisions themselves.

items.title: The zero lower bound isn't quite zero
items.claim: Conventional theory said nominal interest rates couldn't go below zero because cash would dominate negative-rate deposits. What happened in the 2010s?

options.text: Rates never went below zero

Swiss National Bank, ECB, Bank of Japan, Sveriges Riksbank all set negative deposit rates from 2014-16; commercial banks initially absorbed the cost rather than charging retail depositors, due to fear of bank runs and competitive pressure
All countries banned negative rates by law
Cash was abolished worldwide

items.reveal:
Swiss National Bank cut to -0.75% in January 2015. Negative rates persisted in Europe until 2022. The 'effective' lower bound — where negative rates do more harm than good through bank profitability and disintermediation — turned out to be a soft, country-specific constraint rather than a hard zero.

The alternative tools (QE, forward guidance, yield curve control) became more central to monetary policy at the ZLB, raising questions about the toolkit when conventional rate cuts have less room.
items.why: Constraints that look hard in theory often turn out to be empirical and institutional. The ZLB shaped a decade of unconventional monetary policy.

items.title: Forward guidance works only as far as it's believed
items.claim: Central bank forward guidance — communicating future policy intent — has been a key tool since 2008. What's the central credibility problem?

options.text: Forward guidance is legally binding

If markets believe the central bank will deviate from announced policy when conditions change, the guidance has limited effect on long-term rates and expectations — the 'time inconsistency' problem (Kydland & Prescott 1977 Nobel)
Forward guidance always works perfectly
Forward guidance is purely visual

items.reveal:
Kydland and Prescott's 1977 paper formalised time inconsistency: an optimal policy chosen today may not be optimal to follow through later, weakening credibility.

Mark Carney's 'unreliable boyfriend' label (from Pat McFadden MP, 2014) captured a real problem: forward guidance under King and then Carney was reread frequently as conditions evolved. The Fed's 'dot plot' shows committee members' projections without commitment.

State-contingent forward guidance (link to threshold variables) tries to bind more credibly than calendar-based guidance.
items.why: Central bank communication is itself an instrument. Its effectiveness depends on rules versus discretion choices made at the institution level.

items.title: Fiscal multipliers are larger in recessions
items.claim: The IMF's 2012 World Economic Outlook (Blanchard and Leigh) revised fiscal multiplier estimates upward, particularly for recessions. What was the policy implication?

options.text: Austerity was always growth-friendly

Fiscal consolidation in 2010-12 reduced GDP more than initial IMF forecasts assumed (multiplier of ~0.5 in normal times rose to ~1.5+ at the ZLB); contributed to slower recovery, especially in eurozone periphery
Multipliers are always exactly zero
Fiscal policy has no effect on GDP

items.reveal:
Blanchard and Leigh's IMF Working Paper 13/1 acknowledged that the IMF and others had underestimated multipliers in the post-2008 environment. Reinhart-Rogoff's debt-threshold claims also influenced austerity policies that contributed to UK and Eurozone double-dips.

Research since (Auerbach & Gorodnichenko 2012, Ramey 2019) shows multipliers vary with the state of the economy — generally larger in recessions, smaller in expansions or when monetary policy can offset fiscal contraction.
items.why: A single 'multiplier' number hides important variation. The same fiscal policy can have very different effects in different macroeconomic states.

items.title: Automatic stabilisers work without political decisions
items.claim: Unemployment benefits rise automatically in downturns; tax receipts fall as incomes drop. These automatic stabilisers do which of the following?

options.text: Need new legislation each recession

Smooth output and incomes without requiring discretionary decisions, providing counter-cyclical support faster than discretionary stimulus; the IMF estimates they typically absorb 20-50% of GDP shocks in advanced economies
Increase volatility
Only operate during expansions

items.reveal:
OECD analysis: stronger automatic stabilisers (more generous unemployment insurance, progressive taxation) reduce output volatility by ~25%. UK's automatic stabilisers are relatively weaker than the European average.

Discretionary fiscal policy (stimulus packages) is slower (legislation lag, implementation lag) and politically contested. Robert Hall and others have argued for stronger automatic mechanisms as a complement to monetary policy.
items.why: Policy that operates automatically removes one source of delay and politicisation. The design of stabilisers shapes how recessions transmit through the economy.

items.title: The UK's 2010-2015 austerity programme
items.claim: The UK government under Osborne (2010-2016) pursued fiscal consolidation. What was the actual deficit reduction trajectory?

options.text: Deficit was eliminated by 2012
Budget deficit fell from ~10% of GDP (2009-10) to ~4% by 2015-16, but the target of eliminating it by 2015 was missed; growth was slower than OBR projections; public investment was cut sharply
Government spending doubled
Austerity caused immediate hyperinflation

items.reveal:
ONS data: UK fiscal deficit was 10.1% of GDP in 2009-10, 4.1% by 2015-16. The original 2010 emergency budget aimed to balance the structural deficit by 2015; the target was slipped repeatedly.

IFS and OBR analyses found growth fell short of pre-austerity forecasts. Economic historians (Blyth 'Austerity', 2013) and IMF research raised doubts about the timing of consolidation; defenders (Niemietz, others) argued the policy preserved fiscal credibility.

The austerity debate continues; the empirical record is contested but the speed of recovery was slower than baseline.
items.why: Major macroeconomic policy choices have decade-long effects that are hard to evaluate cleanly because counterfactuals are unobservable.

items.title: Comparative advantage is about relative, not absolute, costs
items.claim: Ricardo's 1817 numerical example: Portugal can produce both wine and cloth more efficiently than England (absolute advantage in both). According to comparative advantage, should both countries still trade?

options.text: No — Portugal should produce everything
Yes — both countries benefit from specialising in the good in which they have the lowest opportunity cost. Portugal specialises in wine (relative advantage); England in cloth
Only one country benefits from trade
Trade increases scarcity overall

items.reveal:
Ricardo's 'Principles of Political Economy' (1817) used Portugal-England wine-cloth as a thought experiment, not necessarily descriptive of the actual trade. The insight: even if one country is more productive in everything, gains from trade still arise from differences in relative productivity.

Real-world caveats: factor mobility within countries is imperfect; adjustment costs (displaced workers) can be substantial; gains can be uneven across groups; political economy of trade (David Autor's 'China shock' research on US manufacturing) shows specific losers as well as aggregate gains.
items.why: Comparative advantage is foundational but often taught without the adjustment cost and distributional caveats that determine whether trade liberalisation is politically sustainable.

items.title: FDI flows have plateaued since 2015
items.claim: Global Foreign Direct Investment flows reached record highs in the 2000s. UNCTAD data from 2020 onwards shows what pattern?

options.text: Continued exponential growth
FDI flows have plateaued and partially fragmented along geopolitical lines (US-EU vs China-aligned blocs); 'slowbalisation' or 'fracturing globalisation' is the now-common framing
FDI doesn't exist anymore
All FDI is now in the metaverse

items.reveal:
UNCTAD World Investment Report data: global FDI peaked at $2 trillion in 2015; 2022 flows were $1.3 trillion. Trade as a share of global GDP also flattened.

Drivers: US-China trade tensions (tariffs from 2018), COVID supply-chain reshoring, geopolitical fragmentation (Russia-Ukraine, Taiwan strait), reshoring/nearshoring policies (US CHIPS Act, EU Chips Act, IRA).

The 'end of history' globalisation narrative of the 1990s-2000s has been substantially complicated.
items.why: Globalisation is not a one-way ratchet. The political economy of trade and investment has shifted in ways that affect macroeconomic forecasting and corporate strategy.

items.title: US tariffs on China were largely absorbed by US importers
items.claim: Amiti, Redding and Weinstein (Journal of Economic Perspectives, 2019) studied the incidence of 2018 US tariffs on Chinese imports. What did they find?

options.text: Chinese exporters paid the entire tariff
Nearly the full cost of the tariffs was passed through to US importers and consumers; producer prices in China barely changed. The 'tariffs hurt foreigners' framing did not match the price data
The tariffs raised US incomes
No tariffs were ever imposed

items.reveal:
Amiti, Redding and Weinstein analysed customs and price data through 2019. The pass-through was nearly complete to US importers; Chinese export prices for affected goods didn't drop substantially.

Fajgelbaum, Goldberg, Kennedy and Khandelwal (QJE 2020) confirmed the finding using different methods. Subsequent Biden-era tariffs (2024) followed similar patterns. The US-China tariffs reshaped supply chains (Vietnam, Mexico saw substantial increases in exports to the US) more than they raised significant revenue.
items.why: The political rhetoric of tariffs often diverges from the economic incidence. Trade policy effects are empirically measurable; the empirics often don't support the political framing.

items.title: The impossible trinity constrains exchange rate policy
items.claim: Robert Mundell's impossible trinity (or trilemma) states that a country cannot simultaneously have:

options.text: Inflation, deflation and stagflation
A fixed exchange rate, free capital movement, and an independent monetary policy. It must choose two of three
Both imports and exports
Both fiscal and monetary policy

items.reveal:
Mundell's 1963 paper formalised the trilemma. Choices: fix exchange rate + free capital (give up monetary policy: e.g., classical gold standard, eurozone for individual members); free capital + monetary policy (give up fixed rate: US, UK, Japan); fix exchange rate + monetary policy (give up free capital: China, partly).

The ERM crisis (1992) and the Asian financial crisis (1997-98) both showed the cost of trying to maintain all three. Helene Rey's 2015 work argues that with global financial cycles, even floating exchange rates don't fully restore monetary independence — making the trilemma effectively a dilemma.
items.why: Exchange rate policy isn't a free choice; it's a constrained one. The trilemma sets the menu countries can choose from.

items.title: The Triffin dilemma haunts reserve currencies
items.claim: Robert Triffin's 1959-60 testimony to the US Congress identified a problem with the Bretton Woods system. What was it?

options.text: Gold supplies were too large

The reserve currency issuer (US) had to run current account deficits to supply the world with reserves, but doing so eroded confidence in the currency's gold convertibility — creating a contradiction that would eventually undermine the system
There was nothing to worry about
Only Europe needed reserves

items.reveal_title: Conflict between domestic and international roles
items.reveal:
Triffin published 'Gold and the Dollar Crisis' (1960) elaborating the argument. The Bretton Woods system collapsed in 1971 when Nixon ended dollar-gold convertibility — exactly as Triffin had predicted.

The dilemma persists in modern form: the dollar's global role still requires the US to provide dollar liquidity (via deficits or swap lines), which raises long-run sustainability questions. China's BRICS-related discussions of reserve diversification are a contemporary echo.
items.why: International monetary architecture has structural tensions that don't disappear because the immediate crisis has passed. Triffin remains relevant 60 years on.

items.title: The middle income trap is real but not universal
items.claim: Many countries that reached middle income status (typically $4,000-$12,000 GDP per capita) have struggled to advance to high income. Which describes the phenomenon best?

options.text: All middle-income countries get stuck

A subset (Brazil, South Africa, Argentina, Thailand) have plateaued; others (South Korea, Singapore, Taiwan, more recently Poland) have transitioned successfully. Drivers include education, institutional quality, R&D, and shifting from labour-intensive to knowledge-intensive production
The trap doesn't exist
All countries reach high income automatically

items.reveal:
The term was popularised by Indermit Gill and Homi Kharas's 2007 World Bank study. World Bank research (2013, 2018) found about 13 of 101 middle-income economies in 1960 reached high income by 2008.

South Korea's transition from low- to high-income was unusually rapid (1960-2000). It combined export orientation, investment in education and selective industrial policy. Argentina's reversal (from rich to middle income across the 20th century) shows the direction isn't fixed.
items.why: Development outcomes are heterogeneous. Single-factor explanations (geography, institutions, culture) often capture parts of the story but don't generalise.

items.title: Dutch disease named for Netherlands natural gas
items.claim: The 'Dutch disease' concept emerged from observing the Netherlands after its 1959 Groningen natural gas discovery. What's the mechanism?

options.text: A literal medical condition

Resource exports appreciate the real exchange rate, making non-resource tradable sectors (manufacturing) uncompetitive; when the resource is exhausted or prices fall, the diminished manufacturing base struggles to recover
Excess imports of tulips
Resource discovery always raises GDP permanently

items.reveal:
The Economist coined the term in 1977. Corden and Neary (1982) formalised the mechanism in a two-sector model with traded and non-traded goods.

Observed cases: Netherlands itself (1960s-70s); Venezuela's oil dependence; Nigeria; arguably the UK in the North Sea oil era. Counter-examples (Norway's sovereign wealth fund) show institutional design can mitigate the effect.

The broader 'resource curse' literature (Sachs and Warner, Acemoglu and others) extends to institutional and political channels.
items.why: Natural resource booms are mixed blessings. The institutional and macroeconomic management determines whether they fund long-run development or undermine it.

items.title: Acemoglu and Robinson argue institutions explain development
items.claim: Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson's 2001 AER paper used settler mortality as an instrument for institutional quality. What did they find?

options.text: Institutions have no effect

Places where European settlement was deadly (tropics) developed 'extractive' colonial institutions; places suitable for settlement got 'inclusive' institutions. Institutional differences persist and explain a large share of cross-country income variation today
Only geography matters
Genetics determine institutions

items.reveal:
The 2001 AER paper used settler mortality data to instrument for current institutions (since geography affects mortality but, AJR argue, only affects current outcomes through institutions). Their book 'Why Nations Fail' (2012) developed the inclusive vs extractive institutions framework for a general audience.

Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson won the 2024 Nobel for this body of work. Critics (Glaeser, Sachs) have argued for the role of geography, human capital and culture; the debate over weights between institutional and other factors continues.
items.why: Cross-country growth differences are large and persistent. Identifying causal drivers is genuinely difficult; AJR's instrumental approach was an influential attempt.

items.title: Aid effectiveness — RCTs have refined what we think we know
items.claim: Esther Duflo, Abhijit Banerjee and Michael Kremer won the 2019 Nobel for their experimental approach to development economics. What's the central methodological point?

options.text: All aid is ineffective

RCTs at the village or school level can identify what specific interventions work in specific contexts (e.g., deworming for school attendance, micronutrient supplements), but findings don't necessarily generalise to other settings or scales
All aid programmes have identical effects
Development economics no longer exists

items.reveal:
Banerjee and Duflo's 'Poor Economics' (2011) made the experimental approach accessible. J-PAL (Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab, founded 2003 at MIT) hosts the research network.

Critics (Angus Deaton, 2015 Nobel) argue RCTs are limited in answering 'big' development questions (institutions, macro policy) and that external validity is often weaker than claimed. Both sides agree that aggregate aid effectiveness debates of the 1990s were unresolved by the data of the time.
items.why: Methodological choices shape which questions get answered. The shift to RCTs has produced concrete findings about specific interventions but doesn't directly resolve macro debates.

items.title: Framing changes choices on identical outcomes
items.claim: Kahneman and Tversky's classic 'Asian disease' problem: identical mortality outcomes framed differently (lives saved vs lives lost) produce systematically different preferences. What does this demonstrate?

options.text: People always make consistent choices
Preferences are reference-dependent and influenced by framing: gains and losses are evaluated relative to a reference point, with losses weighted more heavily (loss aversion)
Framing has no effect
All decisions are random

items.reveal:
Tversky and Kahneman's 1981 Science paper presented the Asian disease problem. The same outcomes framed positively (lives saved) vs negatively (lives lost) reversed majority preferences between sure and probabilistic options.

The finding contradicts expected utility theory's invariance axiom. Replications include consumer choice, medical decisions and policy framing. Nudge policy uses this finding by setting defaults (organ donation opt-out vs opt-in) and framing communications.
items.why: If preferences depend on framing, then the framer is a significant agent in any choice architecture. Standard economics' assumed invariance underestimates this.

items.title: Defaults matter — organ donation rates differ by opt-in vs opt-out
items.claim: Johnson and Goldstein's 2003 paper compared organ donation rates in countries with opt-in (default no) vs opt-out (default yes) systems. What did they find?

options.text: Rates were identical regardless of default
Opt-out countries had effective consent rates of 85-99%; opt-in countries 4-28%. The default radically shaped behaviour even when explicit choice was easy
Opt-in countries had higher rates
Both systems produced 50% rates

items.reveal:
Johnson and Goldstein (Science 2003) compared European countries with similar cultures. Germany (opt-in): 12% effective consent; Austria (opt-out): 99.98%. The difference is too large to be preference; it's about the cost of changing the default and what people interpret it as recommending.

The UK moved to opt-out (Wales 2015; England 2020; Scotland 2021) following this evidence. Spain has had high organ donation rates under opt-out plus strong organisational infrastructure for decades.
items.why: Choice architecture has policy effects even when no one's freedom of choice has changed. Defaults are inevitable; designing them deliberately is a choice.

items.title: Thaler's 2017 Nobel marked behavioural economics' mainstreaming
items.claim: Richard Thaler won the 2017 Nobel for contributions to behavioural economics. What's a flagship policy application of his work?

options.text: Setting interest rates

Save More Tomorrow (SMarT) — pension auto-escalation programmes where employees commit in advance to allocate future salary increases to savings. Adoption rates and savings rates rose substantially in trials
International trade theory
Quantum economics

items.reveal:
Thaler and Benartzi's SMarT (2004) is one of the most replicated behavioural interventions. Auto-enrolment to UK workplace pensions (Pensions Act 2008, rolled out 2012-18) raised pension participation from ~55% to ~90%.

The UK's Behavioural Insights Team ('Nudge Unit') was set up in 2010, partly privatised in 2014, now operates internationally. Sunstein worked in the Obama administration on regulatory nudges.

Critics (Gerd Gigerenzer) argue some 'biases' are adaptive heuristics; defenders point to robust effects in field experiments.
items.why: Behavioural economics has moved from contested research programme to standard policy toolkit in two decades. The implementation often outruns settled debates about which biases are 'real' vs adaptive.

items.title: Natural monopolies have decreasing average costs
items.claim: Water supply, electricity distribution and rail track are often described as natural monopolies. What's the defining feature?

options.text: They're nationally owned by law

High fixed costs and economies of scale that extend across the entire market — so a single firm produces at lower average cost than competing firms; competition wastes resources duplicating infrastructure
Government decides them arbitrarily
They have no fixed costs

items.reveal:
UK utility privatisations (1980s-90s) separated naturally monopolistic infrastructure (electricity grids, water distribution, rail track) from contestable elements (generation, supply, train operating companies) and regulated the former.

Ofwat (water 1989), Ofgem (energy 1986), Office of Rail Regulation. RPI-X price controls (Stephen Littlechild's framework) were a UK innovation copied internationally.

New technologies (distributed solar, EVs) are testing whether parts of utility networks remain natural monopolies.
items.why: Market structure isn't only about firm decisions; it reflects cost characteristics. Regulating natural monopolies needs different tools from policing competition.

items.title: Network effects can produce winner-take-all markets
items.claim: A product becomes more valuable to each user as more users join (telephone, social networks, payment platforms). What does this often produce?

options.text: Perfect competition

Strong tendencies to concentration: 'winner-take-all' or 'winner-take-most' markets, often with one or two dominant firms; antitrust intervention becomes harder because consumer prices may be low while market power is high
Constant entry and exit
Many small firms

items.reveal:
Direct network effects: more users → more value (Facebook, WhatsApp). Indirect (cross-side): more buyers attract more sellers and vice versa (Uber, marketplaces).

W. Brian Arthur's 1989 paper on increasing returns formalised the dynamics. Modern antitrust debate (Lina Khan's 2017 'Amazon's Antitrust Paradox') argues consumer-welfare frameworks miss platform power. EU Digital Markets Act (2022) and US recent FTC actions reflect this view.
items.why: Digital markets often don't fit the perfectly-competitive framework of textbook microeconomics. Regulators have had to develop new approaches as a result.

items.title: Switching costs create lock-in even without monopoly
items.claim: Mobile phone contracts, banking services and software subscriptions all create switching costs. How does this affect competition?

options.text: Switching costs always benefit consumers

High switching costs reduce price elasticity, allow price discrimination, and create incumbency advantages; competition can shift from price-on-price to acquisition incentives that don't always benefit existing customers
They have no economic effect
Switching costs only exist in monopoly

items.reveal:
Klemperer's research (1987 onwards) formalised switching cost economics. UK's Open Banking initiative (2018), CASS (Current Account Switch Service 2013) and Ofcom's text-to-switch (2019) all aim to reduce switching frictions specifically.

The CMA's 2016 retail banking market investigation found switching costs and informational frictions sustained higher prices and weak competition.
items.why: Competition exists on a spectrum shaped by frictions. Policy can target the frictions directly (lower switching costs) rather than only firm conduct.

items.title: Price discrimination can be welfare-enhancing
items.claim: A monopolist charges different prices to different consumer groups for the same product. Is this always bad for welfare?

options.text: Yes — always reduces welfare

Not necessarily. Price discrimination can increase output (more consumers served) and total welfare, even when redistributing surplus from consumers to firms. Whether it's welfare-positive depends on demand elasticities and whether output expands
It never affects welfare
It's always welfare-enhancing

items.reveal:
Pigou's 1920 classification: first-degree (perfect, individual reservation prices); second-degree (volume or quality discounts, e.g. Kindle Unlimited tiers); third-degree (group-based, e.g. student/senior pricing, geographic).

Schmalensee (1981) and Varian (1985) showed welfare effects depend on whether discrimination raises total output. Airlines, pharmaceuticals (Ramsey pricing across countries) and education (income-based fee remission) all use price discrimination. Personalisation through data raises new concerns about welfare and fairness.
items.why: Microeconomic textbook intuitions about welfare often need conditioning on output effects. Price discrimination is a clean example of where the textbook needs caveats.

items.title: Perfect competition is a benchmark, not a description
items.claim: Perfect competition (many small firms, homogeneous products, free entry, perfect information) is taught as a foundational market structure. Which is most accurate?

options.text: Most real markets fit the model closely
Real-world markets rarely satisfy the assumptions; agriculture, currency trading and some commodity markets come closer than most. The model is useful as a normative benchmark, not as descriptive
Perfect competition is identical to monopoly
No real-world market resembles it at all

items.reveal:
Monopolistic competition (Chamberlin 1933) and game-theoretic oligopoly models (Cournot 1838, Bertrand 1883, Stackelberg 1934) capture more of the realistic market structures.

Key deviations: most product markets have differentiated products; information is imperfect (Akerlof's 'lemons' 1970); entry has costs; small numbers of dominant firms common. The 'IO revolution' from the 1970s onwards (Tirole's textbook, 1988) built strategic-interaction-based frameworks.
items.why: The perfect competition model serves as a welfare benchmark in policy analysis. Treating it as a description of how markets work misses what most of industrial economics has been building toward.

items.title: Card and Krueger's 1994 paper challenged textbook minimum wage predictions
items.claim: Standard supply-and-demand theory predicts a binding minimum wage reduces employment. What did Card and Krueger's New Jersey study find?

options.text: Employment collapsed

Comparing fast-food employment in NJ (which raised minimum wage) with neighbouring PA (which didn't), they found no significant negative effect on employment, contradicting textbook predictions for the specific context studied
Card and Krueger never studied minimum wages
Wages immediately fell

items.reveal:
Card and Krueger's AER paper used difference-in-differences across the NJ-PA border. Neumark and Wascher's subsequent work using payroll data found small negative employment effects. The literature since has converged on small or moderate effects in the range of minimum wages studied.

Card won the 2021 Nobel for using natural experiments to identify causal effects in labour economics. The minimum wage debate reshaped what economists treat as well-established theory: a 'monopsony' framework (Manning 2003) helps explain why employers may have wage-setting power.
items.why: Empirical economics has overturned several confident textbook predictions through natural experiments. Minimum wage research is the canonical case.

items.title: Carbon pricing is the textbook fix for a textbook problem
items.claim: Climate change is often described as the largest market failure ever (Stern Review 2006). What's the standard economic prescription?

options.text: Government should ignore externalities
Pigouvian carbon pricing (tax or cap-and-trade) to internalise the social cost of carbon emissions; complementary policies for innovation, transition support and distributional fairness
Personal responsibility alone suffices
Markets cannot address environmental issues

items.reveal:
Arthur Pigou's 'Economics of Welfare' (1920) introduced taxes to internalise externalities. William Nordhaus's DICE model (1990s onwards) extended welfare economics to climate; he won the 2018 Nobel.

Real-world implementation: EU ETS (2005, world's largest cap-and-trade); UK Carbon Price Floor; Canada's federal carbon tax; California; Korea. Coverage and prices vary widely. As of 2023, ~25% of global emissions had a carbon price; average price below social cost estimates.

Distributional concerns and political economy of carbon pricing have limited adoption despite theoretical consensus.
items.why: Welfare economics provides a clear policy answer to climate change. Implementation is constrained by political economy more than by economic theory.
